author: Philip K. Dick
date_display: Unpublished in his lifetime; held in the PKD Estate Archives
card_summary: In a future City of Lightness where citizens fly on mechanical wings, Robert Benton is summoned to the Controller's office and told that an invention he has no memory of submitting has been denied: humanity, having reached the absolute limit of its ingenuity a century earlier, adopted 'Stabilization' — a rigidly enforced freeze on all further change, backed by yearly exams, forced disappearances, and a fate called 'the Cart' for those who backslide.
page_summary:
In a future City of Lightness where citizens fly on mechanical wings, Robert Benton is summoned to the Controller's office and told that an invention he has no memory of submitting has been denied: humanity, having reached the absolute limit of its ingenuity a century earlier, adopted 'Stabilization' — a rigidly enforced freeze on all further change, backed by yearly exams, forced disappearances, and a fate called 'the Cart' for those who backslide. Given the model and plans to take home, Benton switches it on and finds it is a time machine. He is flung into a barren, cyclical loop: a field of grain, a forest, a wasteland, and a warning voice telling him not to touch a small glass globe he finds there. He takes the globe anyway and returns to the present — except his return overlaps his own earlier visit to the Controller, so that from the Controller's point of view Benton arrives twice, once with no memory of the second visit yet to come. The globe, containing a shrunken, ancient evil city, has been manipulating him from the start: it engineered his entire encounter with the invention across years in order to be carried out of its glass prison. When Council members come to investigate, the Controller recognizes an old legend just as the globe compels him to smash it. Benton dives to stop him and crushes the globe himself, releasing the city as a mist of whispering, victorious voices that pour into the room and settle over him. The story ends the next morning with Benton marching in ranks to a machine he now serves without memory of having chosen to, wondering only how many weeks remain until his next rest day.

**Why it matters.** As Dick's earliest surviving story, written in high school years before any professional sale, 'Stability' is most valuable as a record of what was already there at the start: a frozen, examination-enforced society; a device that breaks linear time into a loop; and an ending in which the protagonist is hollowed out and turned into an instrument of something else's will, without any dramatic reversal restoring his agency. Those are not incidental juvenile choices — they are the exact triad Dick would spend the next three decades refining. The story's crudeness is real (the globe's plan and its execution are not made to cohere in any rigorous way), but its instincts are already unmistakably his.

*The story does not end with Benton defeating anything. It ends with him marching to work the next morning, wondering about his next rest day — the same small, comfort-seeking man from the opening page, now serving a purpose he cannot remember choosing.*

structure.form: short story in three movements: the frozen society explained, the time loop, the release and possession
movements: The Controller's office: Stabilization explained as the answer to civilization reaching its ceiling.
The invention switched on: a time loop through a dead future, the warning voice, and the globe.
The overlapping return, the globe's true nature revealed, and its release into the world through Benton.
structure.point_of_view: third person close to Benton throughout, so the reader shares his gradual realization that he has been an instrument rather than an agent from the moment the story opened.
structure.structural_device: A closed time loop in which Benton's second visit to the Controller precedes, from the Controller's perspective, the first — the earliest example in this reading of the achronological structure Dick would use throughout his career.

characters.name: Robert Benton
characters.role: citizen of the City of Lightness
characters.note: Ordinary and comfort-seeking at the story's opening ('I don't want it to go to waste'), and entirely hollowed out by its end, marching to a machine 'faithfully' with no memory of ever having chosen to.

characters.name: The Controller
characters.note: The one character who recognizes the ancient legend of the city trapped in glass, and is overridden by the globe's compulsion at the critical moment regardless.

characters.name: The globe / the buried city
characters.note: An imprisoned civilization of 'evil' that spent years orchestrating a chain of cause and effect through an unwitting host to engineer its own release — the story's real protagonist, in the sense that it is the only entity that gets what it wants.

settings.name: The City of Lightness
settings.note: A future built on flight and rigid stasis — technologically fantastic and socially frozen at the same historical moment, a full generation before Dick would make that same combination a signature.

settings.name: The barren future glimpsed through the time machine
settings.note: Grain fields giving way to forest giving way to a dead, level plain — the story's vision of what lies temporally adjacent to Stabilization's frozen present.

settings.name: The Control Offices
settings.note: A vast card-sorting bureaucracy that keeps Stability running, explicitly compared to 'a great symphony orchestra' in which one person out of time would collapse the whole structure.

motifs: Stabilization as the deliberate arrest of civilization's forward motion, enforced by examination and disappearance
A closed causal loop: the effect (Benton's second visit) precedes its own cause from another character's point of view
A voice warning against picking something up, ignored, exactly as in the temptation stories this predates the mature use of
Possession without memory — Benton at the story's end serves a machine, 'faithfully,' having lost all trace of his own volition
Glass as containment for something ancient and hostile, later echoed across Dick's career in objects that turn out to be traps or vessels

distinctive_terms.label: Palm
distinctive_terms.note: The globe resting in Benton's palm — a small but marked image of the trap being held rather than the reverse.

distinctive_terms.label: Fall
distinctive_terms.note: Both the literal fall through the time tunnel and the story's underlying fall-from-stasis anxiety.

distinctive_terms.label: Light
distinctive_terms.note: Named directly in 'the City of Lightness.'

pkd_on_this_work.summary: No direct commentary by Dick on this story was found; the one hit is Sutin quoting the Exegesis on an unrelated topic that happens to share the word 'Stability'.
pkd_on_this_work.gap_noted: As unpublished juvenilia, this story would not appear in Dick's own bibliographic correspondence about sales or anthology contents, which is where most of the 'PKD on his own work' evidence in this project comes from. Any direct comment by Dick on this specific story would most likely surface only in a letter discussing his earliest writing, if one survives.

evidence.author: Lawrence Sutin
evidence.quote: One unpublished SF story — "Stability" — does survive from his high school years, however. "Stability" depicts a post-twenty-fifth-century dystopia governed by the stifling principle of "Stabilization,"
evidence.reading: The essential biographical fact: this is Dick's earliest known story, predating his professional career by roughly five years.

evidence.author: Lawrence Sutin
evidence.quote: "Stability," unpublished short story from high school days, in PKD Estate Archives.
evidence.reading: Sutin's bibliographic entry confirms the archival status directly.

evidence.author: Christopher Palmer
evidence.quote: Other relevant works by Dick are "Stability" (c.1947, CS1), "Prominent Author" (1954, CS2), and Radio Free Albemuth (1985).
evidence.reading: Palmer dates the story to c. 1947 and groups it with two much later works on the strength of a shared concern — the surrounding argument (about images of reading and writing) should be read in full.

contradictions.summary: The story is documented as unpublished archival juvenilia, yet a complete, readable text of it exists in the scanned Collected Stories corpus this project draws on.

claim_a.text: unpublished short story from high school days, in PKD Estate Archives

claim_b.text: a complete 4,831-word text appears in the scanned Collected Stories volume used for this reading

contradictions.note: Not necessarily a real contradiction — 'Stability' may have been included as juvenilia in a later, more complete printing of the Collected Stories than the one Sutin had in mind, or the scan may include material assembled after Sutin's 1989 biography. Worth checking the specific collection volume before treating this text as fully authoritative.

open_questions: Which physical edition of the Collected Stories includes 'Stability', and does its editorial note explain how the juvenile manuscript came to be typeset alongside the professional stories?

Palmer's grouping of this story with 'Prominent Author' and Radio Free Albemuth around 'images of reading and writing' is asserted but not explained in the captured excerpt — the fuller passage would clarify what throughline he sees.
Given how precisely this story anticipates Dick's mature concerns, is there any later interview in which he was asked about his earliest writing and might have mentioned it?

reading_provenance.note: Close reading of the primary text plus attributed evidence from the archive. Candidate: not yet promoted to canonical.

written: c. 1947, while Dick was in high school
critical_caution: Sutin dates this to Dick's high-school years (c. 1947) and describes it as an unpublished manuscript held in the PKD Estate Archives — Dick's earliest surviving story, written years before his first professional sale in 1952. That it appears here as a readable text is notable in itself: this dossier's evidence comes from a scan that included it among the Collected Stories, but its actual publication status is that of unearthed juvenilia, not a magazine sale like the stories around it.
